key_terms.meaning: Model in which matter is treated as continuous, with no gaps between points.
Body whose size is ignored; all forces are taken to act at one point.
Body whose distances between points do not change under load.
Study of bodies at rest or in equilibrium.
Study of bodies in motion or changing motion.
ΣF = ma, where ΣF is net force in N, m is mass in kg, and a is acceleration in m/s².
1 kgf = 9.80665 N, the weight of 1 kg under standard gravity.
Quantity with magnitude only, such as mass or time.
Quantity with magnitude and direction, such as force.
Two vectors from a point are added by the diagonal of the parallelogram they form.
Vector of length 1; F̂ = F/|F| gives the direction of force F.
Splitting a force into components whose vector sum is the original force.
Combining two or more forces into one resultant force.
Forces whose lines of action meet at one point.
Single force that has the same effect as the given force system.
Forces whose lines of action lie in the same plane.
Diagram of a body isolated from supports, showing only external forces on it.
State in which the vector sum of all forces on a particle is zero.
If three coplanar forces on a particle balance, each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two forces is constant.
Cosine of the angle between a vector and a coordinate axis; l = cos θx, m = cos θy, n = cos θz.

takeaways: Ideal models such as the particle and the rigid body make real machines solvable with Newton's laws.
Units must be consistent; use SI N, kg and m/s², and convert kgf to N before calculating.
Forces are vectors, so they add by the triangle or parallelogram law or by components, never by adding their sizes alone.
Resolution and composition are inverse operations; rectangular components use cos and sin of the angle from an axis.
For concurrent coplanar forces, Rx = ΣFx and Ry = ΣFy; the resultant has magnitude √(Rx² + Ry²) and direction tan θ = Ry/Rx.
A free-body diagram shows only external forces after supports are removed, and it is the starting point for equilibrium equations.
A particle is in equilibrium when ΣF = 0, which gives ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 in a plane.
Lami's theorem applies only to exactly three coplanar concurrent forces in equilibrium; in space, equilibrium gives three component equations and a resultant needs direction cosines.
bank_note: Long answers usually test clear definitions, correct free-body diagrams, consistent vector components, and step-by-step equilibrium equations rather than only final numbers.

bank.q: Explain the idealizations used in mechanics, including the particle, the rigid body and the continuum, and state why Newton's laws need consistent units.
outline: Defines mechanics, statics and dynamics
Explains particle as size ignored and rigid body as unchanged distances
Explains continuum model and when it is used
States Newton's laws and gives SI units for force, mass and acceleration
Mentions kilogram-force to newton conversion

bank.q: Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities, and explain addition and subtraction of two forces by the triangle and parallelogram laws.
outline: Defines scalar with examples
Defines vector with magnitude and direction
States triangle law of vector addition
States parallelogram law and diagonal resultant
Explains vector subtraction as addition of the negative vector
Mentions that magnitudes alone cannot be added

bank.q: Explain resolution and composition of forces, with rectangular components of a force F at angle θ to the x-axis.
outline: Defines resolution as splitting a force into components
Defines composition as combining forces into a resultant
Writes Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ
Explains sign convention for components
Shows that vector sum of components gives original force

bank.q: State the component method for the resultant of several concurrent coplanar forces, and explain how a free-body diagram helps set up the components.
outline: Writes Rx = ΣFx and Ry = ΣFy
Writes R = √(Rx² + Ry²) and tan θ = Ry/Rx
Explains choice of x and y axes
Explains isolation of body in a free-body diagram
Mentions that only external forces are shown

bank.q: State the conditions of equilibrium of a particle in a plane and state Lami's theorem with its conditions of use.
outline: Writes ΣF = 0, hence ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0
Explains equilibrium as zero resultant
States Lami's theorem with three coplanar concurrent forces
States that the particle must be in equilibrium
Mentions that Lami's theorem is not valid for four or more forces

bank.q: Forces of 60 N at 0°, 80 N at 60° and 100 N at 150° act at one point. Find the resultant magnitude and direction by the component method.
outline: Resolves each force into x and y components
Adds Rx = 60 + 80 cos 60° + 100 cos 150°
Adds Ry = 0 + 80 sin 60° + 100 sin 150°
Finds R = √(Rx² + Ry²)
Finds θ = tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx) with correct quadrant

bank.q: A force of 500 N acts at 35° above the horizontal. Resolve it into rectangular components and sketch the vector triangle.
outline: Uses Fx = 500 cos 35°
Uses Fy = 500 sin 35°
Calculates Fx ≈ 409.6 N and Fy ≈ 286.8 N
Shows components on a vector triangle
Keeps units in newtons

bank.q: A 10 kg lamp hangs from two strings making 30° and 45° with the horizontal. Draw the free-body diagram and find the tension in each string.
outline: Draws lamp as particle with weight W = 10 × 9.81 N
Shows two tensions along the strings
Writes ΣFx = 0 using T1 cos 30° = T2 cos 45°
Writes ΣFy = 0 using T1 sin 30° + T2 sin 45° = W
Solves for T1 and T2 with units

bank.q: Concurrent forces F1 = 3i + 4j N, F2 = −2i + 5j + 6k N and F3 = i − 3j − 4k N act at a point. Find the resultant and its direction cosines.
outline: Adds components: Rx = 2 N, Ry = 6 N, Rz = 2 N
Finds R = √(2² + 6² + 2²) N
Writes l = Rx/R, m = Ry/R, n = Rz/R
Calculates direction cosines
Checks l² + m² + n² = 1

bank.q: A particle is acted on by F1 = 2i − j + 3k N and F2 = −i + 4j − 2k N. Find the third force needed for equilibrium.
outline: Writes equilibrium condition F1 + F2 + F3 = 0
Finds F1 + F2 = i + 3j + k N
Sets F3 = −(F1 + F2)
Gives F3 = −i − 3j − k N
Checks by adding all three forces

bank.q: Compare the triangle or parallelogram graphical method with the component method for the resultant of concurrent coplanar forces. For eight forces at arbitrary angles, which method is better and why?
outline: Explains graphical method and its scale limitations
Explains component method and its accuracy
Compares effort for many forces
Recommends component method for eight forces
Discusses rounding and sign errors

bank.q: A student applies Lami's theorem to four concurrent forces in equilibrium. Explain why this is invalid, derive Lami's theorem from ΣF = 0 for three forces, and state the conditions under which it can be used.
outline: States Lami's theorem needs exactly three forces
Explains that four forces give four unknowns and need component equations
Derives the sine relation from the force triangle
States coplanar, concurrent and equilibrium conditions
Shows when Lami's theorem gives a quick solution

bank.q: A ring in space is held by three cables and carries a load. Explain how a free-body diagram and three equilibrium equations determine the cable tensions, and interpret a negative tension.
outline: Draws the ring as a particle and marks all cable forces
Writes ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣFz = 0
Explains that three equations solve three unknown tensions
Interprets negative value as compression or wrong assumed direction
Mentions that a cable cannot push, so the model must be checked

bank.q: Explain why direction cosines of a vector satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1, and show how direction cosines give the direction of a resultant force in space.
outline: Defines l = cos θx, m = cos θy, n = cos θz
Uses unit vector components
Shows l² + m² + n² = 1 from unit magnitude
Finds direction cosines from R components
Interprets angles with x, y and z axes

glossary.def: Branch of science that studies forces and the motion or equilibrium they produce.
Study of bodies that are at rest or in equilibrium under forces.
Study of bodies whose motion changes under forces.
Study of motion without considering the forces that cause it.
Study of motion and the forces that produce or change it.
Ideal model in which matter is treated as continuous rather than made of separate particles.
Ideal body with size ignored so that all forces act at one point.
Body in which the distance between any two points remains fixed.
Quantity described by magnitude alone.
Quantity described by magnitude and direction.
Single force that replaces a system of forces with the same effect.
One of two or more vectors whose vector sum equals a given vector.
Process of replacing one force by its components.
Process of replacing several forces by one resultant force.
Forces whose lines of action pass through a common point.
Forces whose lines of action lie in one plane.
Forces whose lines of action lie along the same straight line.
Sketch of an isolated body showing only the external forces acting on it.
Condition in which the vector sum of all forces on a particle is zero.
For three coplanar concurrent forces in equilibrium, each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two is constant.
Cosine of the angle between a vector and a coordinate axis.
Vector with magnitude one, used to show direction.
Rule that adds two vectors by the diagonal of the parallelogram formed from them.
Rule that adds two vectors by placing them head to tail and drawing the closing side.
Force equal to the weight of one kilogram under standard gravity, about 9.80665 N.
SI unit of force; 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
